transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Janine Herbst.
The White House is launching a $25 million program
to reward tipsters who report alleged fraud to the U.S. government.
As part of Vice President Vance's anti-fraud work,
NPR's Emily Fang reports it's in response
to mounting voter concern over perceived government corruption.
A White House official told NPR that the announcement
will be made in the Oval Office this afternoon.
The program will be run by the Department of Justice
and would award up to $30,000 to anyone who submits
a tip that results in a successful fraud conviction.
Vance heads an anti-fraud task force that he claims
has unearthed more than $260 billion in fraud
and federal spending since last January,
though the task force has not provided data for some of the claims
and at least one stems from a Biden-era investigation.
A recent Fox News poll this week found nearly 90 percent
of Americans surveyed were concerned about government corruption,
even more than the percentage concerned about the economy.
Emily Fang, NPR News, The White House.
NPR has learned that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
paid a secret visit to Israel yesterday.
He met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
NPR's Daniel Estrin has more.
There's been no official comment by the U.S. or Israel,
but a person familiar with the matter speaking on condition of anonymity
said Hegseth met with Netanyahu in Israel.
President Trump and Netanyahu have been speaking publicly
suggesting the possibility of a new strike on Iran.
Netanyahu's staff released a video of him next to fighter jets
where he appears to be speaking on the phone with Trump.
Donald, we have a job to finish. You said it and we'll finish it together.
Israel's military announced it's on the highest state of alert
ahead of Israel's elections next week on Tuesday.
Daniel Estrin, NPR News, Tel Aviv.
And President Trump has officially endorsed Netanyahu
in that country's upcoming elections,
but Vice President Vance declined to do so yesterday,
saying he's focusing on American candidates in the midterms.
China says it sent forces to watch a U.S. warship
that entered disputed waters around the Sabina Shoal in the South China Sea.
That shoal is claimed by several countries,
and the surrounding waters have become a flashpoint for regional tensions.
From Taipei, Yan Kamensind Brumby has more.
The Chinese accuse the U.S.S. Charleston of, quote,
"illegally entering the waters around Sabina Shoal."
They accuse the U.S. of infringing on Beijing's sovereignty
as well as undermining stability in the region.
The Philippines meanwhile says the U.S. ship did not enter Chinese territory,
adding that the vessel is traveling in international waters.
The United States has previously been known to carry out
so-called freedom of navigation operations in the region.
Further north in the South China Sea,
Taiwan reports a standoff with the Chinese vessel
around the Taiwan-controlled Pratas Island.
For NPR News, I'm Yan Kamensind Brumby in Taipei.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
Early results show voters in Canada's oil-rich province of Alberta
overwhelmingly backed remaining in Canada
in a referendum yesterday that boosts Prime Minister Mark Carney's push
for national unity.
He says the results allow Canadians to move forward together
and accelerate efforts to diversify trade,
develop infrastructure projects,
and make Canada a global energy powerhouse
amid President Trump's tariffs and annexation threats.
Alberta is home to the world's fourth-largest proven oil fields.
The referendum wasn't a direct vote on independence,
but rather a vote to start the process.
Separatists say many Albertans think the province needs to be treated better.
The Supreme Court is once again taking up the issue of race and school admissions.
This time it's focused on several middle schools in Montgomery County, Maryland,
a suburb of Washington, D.C.
NPR's Sequoia Carillo reports.
Three years after the Supreme Court struck down affirmative action in college admissions,
it will consider the issue of race in admissions for four selective middle schools.
The case focuses on the school's shift to a lottery system
that the county says ensures fair admissions opportunities for all students.
A group of parents who sued disagree.
They say it discriminates based on race,
specifically against Asian American students.
The case has been dismissed twice by lower courts,
but will be argued sometime before the court's term ends next summer.
Sequoia Carillo, NPR News.
While streets trading higher at this hour,
the Dow is up 483 points, the NASDAQ up 18, the S&P 500 up 22.
You're listening to NPR News.

topics.text: White House launches $25 million program rewarding tips on government fraud, run by Justice Department
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth secretly visits Israel and meets Prime Minister Netanyahu, unconfirmed by officials
China sends forces to monitor U.S. warship entering disputed waters near Sabina Shoal in South China Sea
Alberta voters overwhelmingly back remaining in Canada in referendum, boosting Prime Minister Mark Carney
Supreme Court to hear case on race in admissions at Montgomery County, Maryland middle schools
Stock market update: Dow up 483 points, NASDAQ up 18, S&P 500 up 22 in midday trading
